title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM ATHALIAH:
paragraphs:
THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM ATHALIAH:
THE WOMAN WHO KILLED HER OWN FAMILY
There are villains in Scripture who shock us.
But there is one woman whose story feels so dark, so disturbing, and so painfully human that many Christians read her name and quickly move on.
A woman who murdered her own family.
And if we rush past her story too quickly, we may miss one of the most terrifying warnings God ever preserved in His Word.
Because Athaliah's story is not ultimately about politics.
It is about what happens when power becomes more important than people.
When a heart becomes so consumed by control that even family becomes disposable.
And if we are honest, that temptation still exists today.
Not in the form of royal assassinations.
Ways that can quietly destroy marriages, friendships, churches, and even our own souls.
Athaliah appears prominently in 2 Kings 11 and 2 Chronicles 22–23.
To understand her story, we must first understand her roots.
She was connected to the wicked house of Ahab and Jezebel.
Scripture repeatedly portrays that dynasty as one of the most corrupt royal families Israel ever produced.
Their influence was not merely political.
The Hebrew Scriptures often use language that reveals the deeper issue beneath outward behavior.
The Hebrew word for wickedness is often רֶשַׁע (resha‘), referring not merely to mistakes but active rebellion against God's ways.
Athaliah inherited a culture where power mattered more than obedience.
And that is where her story takes a horrifying turn.
"When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family."
"She destroyed all the seed of the kingdom."
The phrase "seed of the kingdom" carries enormous weight.
Every potential heir represented a threat to her throne.
So she attempted to erase them.
Because power had become her god.
Hidden away by faithful people who feared God more than they feared a queen.
For six years Athaliah ruled Judah.
Six years where evil looked like it had won.
This is where many believers struggle.
Because sometimes wickedness appears to prosper.
The faithful hide in the shadows while darkness occupies the throne.
But Scripture repeatedly reminds us that God's silence is never God's surrender.
Psalm 37 repeatedly warns believers not to envy evil people who seem successful because their triumph is temporary.
But she sat on borrowed time.
Eventually the priest Jehoiada revealed young Joash.
And suddenly Athaliah realized everything she had built was collapsing.
The woman who stole a kingdom accused others of stealing it.
The woman who murdered heirs accused others of wrongdoing.
The woman who committed betrayal screamed betrayal.
Sin has a remarkable ability to blind us to ourselves.
The Greek language of the New Testament uses the word τύφλωσις (typhlōsis), meaning blindness or hardening.
That is exactly what sin does.
The greatest danger of sin is not that we see ourselves as evil.
The greatest danger is that we often see ourselves as justified.
Athaliah probably believed she had reasons.
That is why repentance is so difficult.
Repentance requires the death of self-deception.
The New Testament word for repentance is μετάνοια (metanoia).
Her story became a warning preserved forever in Scripture.
But Athaliah's story is not merely about a wicked queen from long ago.
It asks every reader an uncomfortable question.
What am I willing to sacrifice to protect my idols?
Maybe it is always being right.
Maybe it is winning every argument.
Maybe it is preserving an image.
The human heart has not changed nearly as much as we think.
We may not destroy royal heirs.
But people still destroy relationships for power.
Families still fracture because of pride.
Friendships still die because someone refuses to surrender control.
Churches still split because individuals crave influence more than unity.
Athaliah's spirit still appears wherever power becomes more valuable than love.
And that is why the Gospel is such good news.
Jesus is the exact opposite of Athaliah.
Philippians 2 tells us that Christ, though existing in the form of God, humbled Himself.
The Greek word used is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), often translated "emptied Himself."
The innocent died for the guilty.
Athaliah's story shows us what humanity looks like when power reigns.
Jesus shows us what God looks like when love reigns.
One built her kingdom through death.
The other established His Kingdom through His own death and resurrection.
That is the great divide running through all human history.
Perhaps that is why her story remains so unforgettable.
Because somewhere deep inside, we recognize pieces of ourselves.
The temptation to protect our image.
The instinct to preserve ourselves at any cost.
And the Gospel confronts those impulses with a cross.
The cross declares that life is not found through grasping but through surrender.
Not through taking but through giving.
Not through self-preservation but through self-denial.
Athaliah teaches us what happens when power becomes god.
Jesus teaches us what happens when God becomes King.
One is remembered for taking life.
The other is worshiped because He gave His.
And maybe the most sobering lesson of all is this:
The throne you fight hardest to keep may be the very thing keeping you from Christ.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
The most dangerous throne is often the one nobody else can see—the one hidden inside the human heart.
